chapter: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
title: Who led the band at the Tenors; guitarist Willie O'Connor
summary: They try to recall bandleaders at the Tenors and a fine banjo and guitar player who taught others.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: That was John Haynes' band, huh? At the tenors?
Let's see, who had that band that worked at the tenors? No, it was the Louis Daniels. No, wait, what year you was playing at? Oh, I don't know yet. I'll be frank, that's one thing I don't know yet.
Because Kuyper was there for a while. When I was at the tenors? No, no, no. You came after the kind of thing.

When I was in there it was a guitar player, a band-a-gill player's job. For that one? For that one. He taught René Hall and all them for that. He was a very good band-a-gill player and guitar player. What was his name? Willie what? Willie O'Connor. Willie O'Connor. Yeah. Willie O'Connor.
Client and piano and the greatest, one of the greatest alto players that ever put an alto

to his mouth. No, no, no. I don't want you. You never met him? Just unassumable as can be, but the finest play you ever play? He never smiled. He's a phenomenal. I'm a smart guy. He's a nice fellow. And even one of the fun times we would have, in fact I would have so many different times I wouldn't know exactly when we'd stop working on that because it'd be one place and there'd be another. We'd work at the, what was it, the Papaw? Oh, Decatur Street. Yeah. Papaw and Decatur Street. We worked at the Lake, remember? That's right. Right near the happening, I don't know what the name was, the place. Mamalu. No, now you're talking about Mamalu. It must be, it suits you. No, you remember when you were- Moro. Yeah, that's right. Moro. Uh-huh. Because every time we look, I was going with Harold someplace.
